blocks.text: During interphase chromatin is duplicated: the DNA replicates and new histones are made. Afterwards each chromosome consists of two identical strands, the sister chromatids, attached at a constricted region called the centromere. The centromere is a specific DNA sequence of about 220 nucleotides. A disc-shaped protein structure, the kinetochore, is attached to the centromere; it is where the chromosome attaches to the spindle during cell division.

blocks.alt: Left: a duplicated chromosome made of two sister chromatids joined at a centromere with a kinetochore disc; near the top a secondary constriction separates a small knob, the satellite; the ends are telomeres. Right: four duplicated chromosomes with the centromere in the middle (metacentric), a little off-centre (sub-metacentric), near one end (acrocentric) and at the end (telocentric).
blocks.caption: A duplicated chromosome and the four types by centromere position (original diagram after Figures 19.1 and 19.2).
blocks.long_description: After DNA replication in interphase each chromosome consists of two identical sister chromatids attached at a constricted region, the centromere, a specific DNA sequence to which a disc-shaped protein, the kinetochore, is attached; spindle fibres attach at the kinetochore during division. Some chromosomes have a secondary constriction, the nucleolar organizer region, which makes nucleoli in interphase, and the knob-like end beyond it is the satellite. The ends are telomeres, which stop chromosomes sticking to each other end to end. By centromere position chromosomes are metacentric, sub-metacentric, acrocentric or telocentric.

items: Secondary constriction (nucleolar organizer region, NOR): a second constriction in some chromosomes, which makes nucleoli during interphase.
Satellite: the knob-like end of the chromosome beyond the secondary constriction; this region has highly repetitive DNA sequences, called junk DNA.
Telomeres: the terminal ends of chromosomes, which prevent two chromosomes from attaching to each other by their ends.

blocks.title: Tidbit
blocks.text: Chromosomes were discovered by the German embryologist Walther Flemming in 1882, in the rapidly dividing cells of salamander larvae. The name 'chromosome', literally 'coloured bodies', was proposed by the German anatomist Waldeyer-Hartz in 1888.
